summary:
Kwara State stands under Nigeria's national framework rather than any regional exception. It is not among the twelve states recorded as having adopted Sharia law — Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara — so no Sharia penal exposure, including the death penalty prescribed under state Zina provisions for male sodomy, is documented for the Ilorin area. The federal statute supplies the operative framework.

The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, signed in January 2014, applies nationwide and carries up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity under federal law. The Criminal Code operates in southern states and the Penal Code in northern states. The Act voids same-sex unions, criminalises forming, operating or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and Human Rights Watch records a penalty range of 10 to 14 years for participating in or supporting such groups. It also bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's updated travel advice for Nigeria, reported on 19 August 2026, warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation; of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity; of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in some northern states; and of the Act's reach to helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBT+ people.

Enforcement is documented as arbitrary and extortionate rather than procedural. Human Rights Watch records mob attacks, arbitrary arrests, extortion and detentions of LGBT people across Nigeria following the Act's passage, including 21 young men arrested and never charged at a birthday gathering in Ibadan. News coverage in August 2024 reports that mass arrests and detention of LGBT people are common, especially in northern states. No Kwara-specific case appears in these sources.

Trans people in Nigeria face lethal violence. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama was found on a highway in Abuja and police opened an investigation; she had been stabbed a year earlier and had feared for her life.

In 2022 a court ruled Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Act unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide.
tangentialFactors:
Kwara's position outside the Sharia belt removes the capital-penalty exposure that applies in the twelve northern states, but the federal statute reaches every state, so the 14-year ceiling and the ancillary bans on organising, cohabitation and public displays apply in Ilorin as they do in Lagos or Abuja.

Documented enforcement in non-Sharia states shows the risk is not confined to the north: the 21 men arrested and never charged at a birthday gathering in Ibadan were held in a south-western state operating under the Criminal Code, and the extortionary stop described in other reporting occurred in Lagos.

News reporting indicates that mass arrests and detention of LGBT people are concentrated especially in northern states, which suggests a heavier day-to-day enforcement climate there than in Kwara, without reducing the statutory exposure in Kwara itself.

The August 2024 killing of a 33-year-old transgender woman in the national capital, a year after she was stabbed and while she feared for her life, evidences a pattern of violence against trans people that is national rather than local, and one in which police involvement followed the death rather than preceding it.

The 2022 ruling striking three sections of the Act coexists with continued arrest, extortion and detention documented afterwards, so constitutional invalidation of those provisions has not produced a demonstrably lower enforcement risk for visitors.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kwara State are exposed to the same federal statute as the rest of Nigeria: up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex sexual activity, 10 to 14 years for participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations, and criminal liability for same-sex cohabitation and public shows of a same-sex amorous relationship. Same-sex unions are void.

The Act's helpers-and-attendees provision extends liability beyond couples to anyone who assists at or attends a same-sex wedding.

Arbitrary enforcement carries a direct financial dimension for residents. Human Rights Watch documents extortion alongside arbitrary arrest and detention across the country after the Act's passage, and mob attacks on LGBT people followed the law's introduction.

No Kwara-specific arrest, prosecution or detention case is documented in these sources; the national reporting names cases in Ibadan, Abuja and Lagos. Residents therefore face the federal statute with no locally sourced record of how Kwara police apply it.

No hate-crime protection, anti-discrimination protection or other legal remedy for sexual orientation or gender identity is recorded for residents in these sources.

The sources state that the Criminal Code operates in southern states and the Penal Code in northern states, but do not place Kwara within either column, and Kwara's status as a north-central state is not settled by the material here.

Unresolved: the practical effect of the 2022 ruling declaring Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide. The sources do not state which conduct those sections covered, whether the ruling was appealed, or whether police continue to arrest under them.

Unresolved: whether proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public have been enacted. Reporting from 2022 records that transgender Nigerians feared such proposals; the material available here does not settle their status.

Not sourced: any Kwara-specific data on document or marker rules for trans visitors, entry and visa screening, bathroom or facilities access, gender-affirming care, housing of trans detainees, or partner recognition. The Bobrisky imprisonment reported nationally concerned a naira abuse sentence and does not establish Kwara practice on placement between male and female sections.

Not sourced: any count of arrests, prosecutions or convictions in Kwara under the Act, or any statement by Kwara State authorities on enforcement policy.
